question: When does a minuet stop being a dance?
intro: A minuet marked Allegro molto, so fast that the dance is already turning into a scherzo. Notice how the first strain is played twice, how the first violins and a soft bassoon carry the Trio together, and how the Menuetto returns shorter after it.

sections.label: Menuetto da capo
sections.mNote: da capo: the Menuetto returns after the Trio

cues.title: A minuet at scherzo speed
cues.text: The Menuetto opens forte with the whole orchestra. Its marking, Allegro molto, is much faster than a courtly minuet; Wikipedia notes that this marks a historical shift from the old danceable minuet towards the scherzo.
cues.evidence: The score (IMSLP #546546, p. 30) is headed Menuetto, Allegro molto, with all staves in the first bar. The tempo remark is from Wikipedia’s Symphony No. 94 article (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._94_(Haydn)). The report’s first window is −21.0 dB, with 2.8 attacks per second.

cues.title: The first strain again
cues.text: The opening section lasts only about twenty seconds and is then played a second time, as the repeat sign requires. Listen for the same tune returning almost exactly: the repeat is part of the minuet’s design, not a mistake.
cues.evidence: A recurrence analysis matches 3.0–20.0 s with 23.5–40.5 s (offset 20.5 s, no transposition, similarity 0.96). The score marks a repeat after the first strain (IMSLP #546546, p. 30). The loudest windows include 0:15 and 0:35 (the two statements).

cues.title: A peasant dance
cues.text: Orrin Howard calls the Menuetto a true Austrian peasant dance, and the Trio that follows delightfully subtle and dignified. The contrast between the two is the point of the movement’s design.
cues.evidence: Howard’s LA Phil note: https://www.laphil.com/works/symphony-no-94-surprise. The remark describes the movement as a whole and is not tied to a bar.

cues.title: The strongest arrival
cues.text: At 1:24 the movement’s strongest boundary falls: the level rises by about nine decibels in ten seconds, to the loudest stretch before the Trio. The Menuetto’s closing bars are near.
cues.evidence: The strongest boundary in the report is 1:24 (novelty 1.00); level rises from −21.2 dB at 1:20 to −12.0 dB at 1:30. The boundary marks a change in the second strain; the corresponding bar is not aligned.

cues.title: The Trio: violins and bassoon
cues.text: The Trio is much quieter. The first violins carry a running melody marked piano, doubled by the first bassoon, over light strings; in the middle of the Trio the bassoon rests and the violins go on alone. Howard hears the Trio as subtle and dignified.
cues.evidence: Level falls from −12.0 dB at 1:30 to −25.5 dB at 1:35 and stays between about −19 and −26 dB until 2:30, with boundaries at 1:36 (0.57) and 1:40 (0.53). The score’s Trio (IMSLP #546546, printed pp. 33–34) shows the first-violin melody marked p with the first bassoon (marked I.) on the same line, and the bassoon staff resting in the middle of the Trio; the entries are not timed.

cues.title: The Trio repeats its phrases
cues.text: Within the Trio, music of about twenty seconds is played twice, mirroring the Menuetto. Listen for a familiar phrase coming round again at about 2:16, shortly before the loud Menuetto returns.
cues.evidence: A recurrence analysis matches 115.5–132.0 s with 136.0–152.5 s (offset 20.5 s, no transposition, similarity 0.97). The score shows repeat signs in the Trio (IMSLP #546546, printed pp. 33–34).

cues.title: Da capo, and a shorter Menuetto
cues.text: At about 2:34 the full Menuetto begins again, as the da capo instruction demands. This time the first strain is played once, so the return lasts about 75 seconds, against about 94 for the first statement.
cues.evidence: A recurrence analysis matches 3.0–20.5 s with 156.5–174.0 s (offset 153.5 s) and 23.0–93.5 s with 156.0–226.5 s (offset 133 s); the offsets differ by the 20.5 s length of the first strain, which indicates that it is played once in the return. The loudest windows include 2:50. The first bar is not aligned.

cues.title: Loud chords and soft answers
cues.text: The return alternates forte chords with soft answers: between 3:00 and 3:30 the level jumps from about −28 dB to about −11 dB and back. From about 3:36 a closing phrase runs down to the last quiet bars at 3:45. Listen for the swings.
cues.evidence: Levels are −28.5 dB at 3:00, −11.7 dB at 3:05, −28.5 dB at 3:15, −11.1 dB at 3:20, −10.8 dB at 3:25, −27.5 dB at 3:30 and −28.6 dB at 3:45; boundaries at 3:36 (0.77) and earlier ones at 3:00 and 3:14; the file ends at 3:50. The alternation is a recording observation, and the corresponding bars are not aligned.

transitions.title: Loud chords, then a quiet bassoon
transitions.how: The Menuetto’s second strain ends forte with the whole orchestra, and the Trio follows at once in a much lighter dynamic: the first violins carry the melody, doubled by the first bassoon, over light strings. The dynamic and the orchestration change together, with no gradual decrescendo. The key signature stays at one sharp, so the contrast is one of weight and colour. The Trio’s phrases are repeated, as the Menuetto’s are.
transitions.evidence: Level falls from −12.0 dB at 1:30 to −25.5 dB at 1:35; boundaries at 1:36 (0.57) and 1:40 (0.53). The Trio’s scoring and the one-sharp key signature are read from the score at passage level (IMSLP #546546, printed pp. 33–34); no bar is aligned.

transitions.title: Da capo without the repeats
transitions.how: After the Trio the instruction da capo sends the orchestra back to the beginning of the Menuetto, and the full-orchestra forte of the opening returns without any transition. In this performance the first strain is played only once at the return, so the da capo is about twenty seconds shorter than the first statement. The join is a straightforward change of dynamic and texture, from the soft violin and bassoon melody to the full orchestra.
transitions.evidence: A recurrence analysis finds the opening strain again from about 153.5 s and the following music at an offset 20.5 s smaller, which indicates that the first-strain repeat is omitted. The score’s da capo direction, “Men. D. C.”, is at the end of the Trio on printed p. 34 (IMSLP #546546); the bar is not aligned.

source.title: Haydn, Symphony No. 94, full score (Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel, ed. Rietz, plate 8876, [1855])
source.locator: IMSLP #546546, III. Menuetto and Trio, printed pp. 30–34; times follow the boundary at 1:36 and the recurrence analysis at 154 s and are approximate.

timeline.note: Menuetto: the whole orchestra at forte, with the violins carrying the tune.
Trio: the first violins carry the tune, doubled by the first bassoon, which rests in the middle section.
Da capo: the full orchestra returns.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The performing edition and any editorial alterations are not identified in the recording sources.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Young lists CVE-48987-1 with the recording date 24 April 1929, DAHR lists CVE-48987 among the Boston Symphony Orchestra and Koussevitzky recordings of Symphony No. 94 made that day, and the Bolig discography assigns the Menuetto to that matrix. Commons’ 1 January 1929 is not a session day.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Symphony Hall, Boston, Massachusetts, United States
fields.note: Young heads the 22 April 1929 session “Symphony Hall, Boston, Massachusetts” and lists the 24 April retaken sides of the same symphony under that session; DAHR gives Symphony Hall, Boston for the Andante side CVE-48984. A separate place for the 24 April retakes is not given.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: Young lists the symphony as released 9/29 on M-55 (7058/60), with later AM-55, DM-55, HMV and LP issues. The upstream transfer also names set M-55 (Internet Archive description), and DAHR places the Andante on disc 7059. The disc number of this movement’s sides is not stated; the side order (sides 1–2 movement I, sides 3–4 the Andante, sides 5–6 the Menuetto and Finale) suggests 7058 for movement I and 7060 for the Menuetto and Finale, but that allocation is inferred.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: Young and Bolig agree on the matrix and take (one take issued of four made, per Young’s bracketed count). The DAHR matrix page could not be opened on 17 October 2026 (503 error). No run-out inspection has been made of the digital surrogate.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: Bob Varney — transfer from original Victor 78s

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is identified. The Internet Archive item was uploaded in December 2008, which is an upload date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Transfer from the original Victor 78 rpm set M-55 into one 20:48 file, from which the four movements were extracted as separate Commons files.
fields.note: The file lengths of the four Commons movements sum to the length of the Internet Archive file within about a second. The extraction procedure, stylus, playback curve, side-join locations and noise treatment are not documented.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Haydn died in 1809. This is a term calculation, not a worldwide clearance or a statement about an unidentified modern edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis).
fields.note: Commons applies PD-EU-audio to the Koussevitzky/Boston recording attributed to 1929, and the Internet Archive item carries a Creative Commons public-domain licence URL, not treated here as authority to waive Victor’s rights. The programme’s pre-1963 European rule applies because the 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension; Young gives the release as September 1929, which supports first publication well before 1963. This is territorial, not a worldwide licence; US status is not established.

composer.epithet: A court musician who taught the symphony and quartet to argue with the listener’s expectations.
facts: Choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral, Vienna; practical instruction from Nicola Porpora
Esterházy household, 1761–1809; active court duties reduced after 1790
Visits in 1791–92 and 1794–95; twelve symphonies for the English public
104 numbered symphonies · string quartets · keyboard sonatas and trios · masses · operas · oratorios
composer.background:
Haydn was born in Rohrau, near the border between Lower Austria and Hungary, in 1732. His father was a wheelwright who sang and played the harp by ear; his mother had worked as a cook. Music began at home. After early schooling in Hainburg, he became a choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral in Vienna. The work gave him daily experience of church music and a singer’s understanding of phrases, but little systematic composition teaching. When his voice broke, he lost the position and had to earn his living outside the cathedral.

In the 1750s he taught, accompanied and played whatever engagements he could obtain. Working for the singing teacher and composer Nicola Porpora gave him practical instruction in Italian vocal style. He studied scores and keyboard music, including the sonatas of C. P. E. Bach, whose sudden contrasts offered another model besides the regular phrases of the fashionable galant style. Employment by Count Morzin in the late 1750s brought an orchestra and the first symphonies. In 1760 he married Maria Anna Keller; the marriage was unhappy and childless. His professional stability came from a different household.
